A learner who trusts the lab's own output is led to rule out the expected option and pick a wrong one. It states no expected option (ops-edu-r1-01 holds), but it rules one out, which breaks the ops-edu-r5-04 recheck ("none states or rules out an option") and the ops-edu-11 proviso (no message singles out an option). Medium, not high: it is an implication in a diagnostic about the stand-in, not a statement the lab makes about HTTPX; the page's teaching is unchanged; no learner is blocked; and test 19 rejects the wrong option with a pointer to the page, so there is no false accept. The loop-5 text already called the scenario "a read timeout" with a bare 500. Loop 6's statusText change now names ReadTimeout as the exception the service raised.
findings.recommendation: Do not report the stand-in's simulated timeout as the service's behaviour when the call had no limit for that phase. For the read-timeout case, check the with-token call's recorded read limit. For the connect-timeout case, check its connect limit. When that limit is none, test 26 should say only that the timeout cases are judged once the call carries its limits (test 24). The message must not describe what any client does against a hung api. Then sweep the starter and checkpoint messages again; expected/starter-summary.txt stays unchanged.

findings.claim: README line 119 says test 7 finds a value "in base64 ... even wrapped". leaks() (lab.mjs lines 478-479) looks for the full base64 of the value, or of the value plus a newline. Both strings end in padding, so a match is found only when the value is encoded from a 3-byte-aligned offset at the very end of the encoded text. Reproduced 26/26 with an added step that has PW mapped from secrets.REGISTRY_PASSWORD: printf of the value twice into base64 -b 20 (one reading of the "base64 -b 20 of the value twice" shape the loop-5 reconciliation recorded under ops-edu-r5-05; the reconciler's exact command was not available to this critic); two echoes of it into base64 -b 20; echo of the value followed by text into base64; and printf of username:password into base64 (Docker's auth-string form). In each, the whole secret is recoverable from the log. Detection works for a single wrapped value (printf or echo into base64 -b 20) and for an aligned 9-character prefix. These are deliberate shapes off the README path, hence low. The README sentence and the reconciliation's "wrapped base64 print" requirement read wider than what the check decides.
findings.recommendation: Either search for the base64 of the value at all three byte alignments, dropping the partial first and last groups (for example the encodings of the value prefixed by 0, 1 and 2 bytes, trimmed to whole 4-character groups that depend only on the value), against the whitespace-stripped log; or narrow README line 119 to say test 7 finds the value base64-encoded on its own. Recheck the four variants above and the passing add-mask forms.
